hook: Spain expels its Jews, and ships reach the Americas; both shaped centuries of suffering

segments.voice: Yesterday, Michelangelo: a painted finger, and the hand of God reaching for it. Your line was almost touching. What was almost within reach yesterday? Day eight hundred thirty-seven.

Two documents from one year. The first is a royal decree, signed by Ferdinand and Isabella, the king and queen of Spain. It orders every Jew in their kingdoms to leave by a fixed deadline and never return. Only baptism would let a family stay. The second is the opening of a sailor's journal. Christopher Columbus writes to those same two monarchs, and in a single stretch of thought he mentions the Jews being driven out, and his own orders to sail west. Same rulers. Same year. Same page. Today's word is Sephardic.
screen: `A DECREE: LEAVE, AND NEVER RETURN.` → `A SAILOR'S JOURNAL.` → `SAME RULERS, SAME PAGE.`

segments.voice: Start with the decree. Jewish families had lived in Spain for generations: doctors, weavers, translators, neighbors. Now they had until the deadline to choose. Some were baptized and stayed, and they and their children often lived afterward under suspicion from the Inquisition. Others sold what they could, left homes and graves behind, and went out to Portugal, North Africa, the lands of the Ottoman sultan. Their descendants, called Sephardic Jews, carried the language and songs of Spain with them. Next, the journal. Columbus reaches an island in the Caribbean, and the people there, the Taíno, come out to meet the ships. He writes that they are gentle, that they carry no weapons, and almost in the same breath that they would make good servants. That sentence turned out to be a forecast. What followed for the peoples of the islands and the mainland was forced labor, war and disease, and whole communities were lost. Then, the hard part for Catholics. Both stories were told by their tellers in the language of faith. The decree spoke of protecting the faith; the voyage spoke of carrying it. Catholic teaching today says plainly that faith must never be forced, and recent popes have asked forgiveness for wrongs done by the Church's members. Finally, the word for today. Remembering honestly is not the same as hating the past. It means letting both documents stand, without cutting either. Psalm one hundred twenty-nine begins, "Out of the depths I have cried to thee, O Lord: Lord, hear my voice." It is a prayer that fits exiles. It fits people whose land was taken, too. Honest memory makes room for both voices.
screen: `A DECREE, AND FAMILIES ON THE ROAD.` · `GENTLE PEOPLE, AND A FORECAST.` · `BOTH TOLD IN THE LANGUAGE OF FAITH.` · `LETTING BOTH DOCUMENTS STAND.` · then, large: `OUT OF THE DEPTHS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold the descendants of both. Settle, and breathe slowly. First, bring to mind the Jewish families who walked out of Spain, and the families today who come from them. Stay there a few breaths. Then bring to mind the Taíno and the peoples of the Americas, and those living today who come from them. If you pray, you can pray for both, using the psalm's words, out of the depths. If you don't, simply hold the two groups of people in your attention, one after the other, without hurrying. The bell holds the time.
Sephardic. The name for the Jews exiled from Spain in 1492, who carried its language and songs into exile. Today's word.
Your line: remember honestly. Today, when a story gets told about the past, at work or at home, ask once: who else was there, and how would they tell it? Day eight hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Catholic memory of these wrongs is public as well as personal: John Paul II's Day of Pardon in the Jubilee year 2000 confessed sins against the people of Israel and against the rights of peoples, and Pope Francis has asked forgiveness for crimes against the native peoples of the Americas during the conquest.

fork.setup: you're a Jewish weaver in Spain. the decree is read in the square: leave by the deadline and never return. only baptism lets you stay. what do the families around you do?
options: some are baptized and stay; others sell what they can and go.
the decree is withdrawn before the deadline.
fork.reveal: both happened. some were baptized and stayed, often under suspicion; others left homes and graves behind for Portugal, North Africa and the Ottoman lands.

trapdoor: what you thought: 1492 is the year Columbus sailed.
what it means: the same rulers, in the same year, also drove Spain's Jews into baptism or exile.
what a scholar hears: the two stories touch in Columbus's own journal, which names the expulsion and his commission together in its opening lines.

notes: The year 1492 is the index word and the date of both cited documents; no other dates or counts are given in the voice. The index hook's 'centuries of suffering' is not stated as a count.
Decree: Jews to convert or leave by a deadline (about four months; 'a few months' in the voice). Confirm wording.

Columbus's journal survives through Las Casas's abstract; the prologue links the expulsion of the Jews 'in the same month' with the monarchs' commission, and the October 12 entry describes the Taíno as gentle, unarmed, and fit to be 'good servants'. Paraphrased; confirm, and consider noting the abstract in the voice.
Destinations of Sephardic exiles (Portugal, North Africa, Ottoman lands) and 'lived under suspicion from the Inquisition' for conversos: confirm phrasing.

'Recent popes have asked forgiveness for wrongs done by the Church's members' alludes to John Paul II's Day of Pardon (2000) and Francis's apologies to Indigenous peoples; not cited as a text. Confirm or cite.
Dignitatis Humanae 10 on faith not being forced: paraphrased. Confirm.

Editor: the decree now 'orders every Jew to leave ... never return', with baptism as the only way to stay (the edict's text orders expulsion and does not itself offer baptism); hook screen, myth and fork changed to match. 'A few months' cut per the claims rule. 'Exiles sang that kind of prayer' (unsourced) softened to 'a prayer that fits exiles'.
Editor (second pass): fixed a missing space in the hook screen string.

Auditor: howItsDone's unsourced claim that parishes and dioceses 'hold services of memory and reconciliation' replaced with the two documented papal acts (Day of Pardon, 12 March 2000; Francis in Bolivia, July 2015). Confirm wording.
